title: New Barossa Restaurant The Curry Lab Revives Forgotten Indian Spices in Nuriootpa
excerpt: Run by 24-year-old Shan and his parents, the Nuriootpa restaurant pairs family recipes with an interactive spice library where diners can smell the ingredients behind the menu.
body:
• The Curry Lab, a family-run Indian restaurant, opened in Nuriootpa in the Barossa Valley on September 17, run by 24-year-old Shan and his parents.
  • The restaurant centers on Indian spices that have fallen out of modern cooking, including ratanjot, rose petals and yellow mirch.
  • A signature feature is an interactive "spice library" where diners can smell the ingredients behind the menu.
  • The family already owns Zest Cafe in Clare; The Curry Lab is their first dedicated Indian restaurant in regional South Australia.

There is a new Indian restaurant in the Barossa Valley, and it smells like an education. The Curry Lab officially opened in Nuriootpa on Thursday, September 17, at 18–28 Tanunda Road — a family-run restaurant built around a simple idea: bringing forgotten Indian spices back to the table.

The restaurant is run by 24-year-old Shan and his parents. For Shan, the opening is the realization of a long-held family plan. The family already owns Zest Cafe in Clare, which Shan says has let them share some Indian food with customers — but The Curry Lab goes much further, into the regional cooking of his own heritage.

"We've always imagined opening an Indian restaurant in regional South Australia."

— Shan, owner, The Curry Lab

A family kitchen, scaled up

Shan grew up in Whyalla before travelling overseas and working in restaurants and hospitality, alongside formal study in cooking. His Indian heritage sits at the center of the new restaurant: he was born in Jharkhand, where his mother was also born, while his father is from Lucknow in Uttar Pradesh. The cooking, he says, started in the family kitchen.

"Every time my mum was in the kitchen, I would be helping her cook everything," he told Glam Adelaide. "In cooking, I would say it's this thing that brings everyone together, especially for me and my family."

That sensibility shapes the menu. Rather than the familiar curry-house canon, The Curry Lab's dishes incorporate ingredients that have become less common in modern Indian cooking — ratanjot, the alkanet root that lends a deep red color; rose petals; and yellow mirch, a dried yellow chilli. These are ingredients from family recipes and regional traditions, not the standardised pantry of restaurant Indian food.

The spice library

The restaurant's biggest point of difference, according to its owners, is an interactive "spice library" where diners can smell the ingredients behind the menu. The idea is part theater, part education: before ordering, guests can handle and smell the raw spices that will season their food — a direct line between the unfamiliar name on the menu and the aroma in the bowl.

For a wine region built on tasting notes and provenance, the concept fits. The Barossa draws visitors who already think about flavor in terms of origin and process. The Curry Lab applies that logic to spices most Australians have never encountered by name.

Why it matters

Indian restaurants in regional Australia often hew to a narrow, crowd-tested menu. The Curry Lab is a bet that regional diners — and the Barossa's food tourists — are ready for something closer to the source: family recipes, lesser-used spices, and a young owner cooking the food he grew up with.

It also continues a quiet trend of Indian-Australian families moving from cafes and takeaways into chef-driven regional dining, carrying their own food traditions into communities where Indian food was previously a Friday-night takeaway.

What's next

The Curry Lab is now open in Nuriootpa. The family has not announced further venues, but Shan's framing suggests this is the start of something larger: an Indian restaurant identity for regional South Australia that begins, fittingly, with the spices most people have forgotten.
